Compunction is the uneasy, guilty feeling you get in your conscience when you have done something wrong — or when you are about to do something wrong and some inner voice tells you that you shouldn't.

Think of it as your moral conscience giving you a sharp little pinch from the inside.

Compunction is not just a passing thought like "Hmm, maybe that wasn't great." It carries a genuine sense of moral discomfort — a quiet but real weight on your mind that comes from knowing your action crossed a line. It is the feeling that something you did (or are considering doing) was not right, and that feeling troubles you.

For example: You gossiped about a close friend behind their back. Later, you feel a gnawing sense of guilt — that is compunction. Or imagine you are about to cheat on a test, and something inside you hesitates, makes you uneasy, makes you feel bad even before you do it — that hesitation is also compunction.

So it works in two directions:

  • Looking back — guilt and remorse over something already done.
  • Looking forward — moral unease that makes you hesitate before doing something you know is wrong.

You will encounter this word most often in the phrase "without compunction" — and understanding this phrase is key to truly owning this word.

When someone does something without compunction, it means they do it with no guilt whatsoever — no hesitation, no inner conflict, no moral discomfort. The phrase often carries a cold or even chilling tone, because it implies the person either doesn't care that their action is wrong, or doesn't even recognize it as wrong.

"The dictator ordered the executions without compunction."
"She lied to him without compunction."
"He threw years of friendship aside without compunction."

In each case, the absence of compunction is what makes the action feel ruthless, callous, or morally alarming.

Compunction can be mild or strong. Writers and speakers often signal the intensity through the words they pair with it:

  • A twinge of compunction — just a small, brief flicker of guilt. Barely noticeable.
  • A pang of compunction — a sharper, more sudden burst of guilt.
  • Deep compunction / profound compunction — serious, heavy guilt that weighs on a person.
  • No compunction / without compunction — zero guilt at all.

"He felt a slight twinge of compunction after snapping at his younger brother, but shook it off quickly."
"She experienced a deep compunction over the way she had treated him all those years."

Since you are learning this word fully, it helps to see clearly how it sits among its neighbors:

Compunction vs. Guilt
Guilt is the broader, everyday word. Compunction is more specific and more formal. Guilt can be a general state; compunction is more of a moment — a specific feeling pricking your conscience about a specific act.

Compunction vs. Remorse
Remorse is deeper and heavier. Remorse usually comes after a serious wrong, and it lingers. Compunction is lighter and quicker — it can be just a fleeting moral discomfort. You might feel compunction about a small lie; you feel remorse about something truly serious.

Compunction vs. Regret
Regret is wider in meaning. You can regret things that had nothing to do with right or wrong — like missing a flight, or not learning to play the guitar. Compunction is specifically moral — it is always tied to the sense that something was ethically wrong.

Compunction vs. Qualm
A qualm is a feeling of doubt or unease, and it can be moral, but it can also be non-moral (e.g., feeling nervous or uncertain). Compunction is exclusively moral — it is always about right and wrong.

Compunction vs. Scruple
This is the closest cousin. A scruple is a moral principle that stops you from doing something. Compunction is the feeling of guilt or unease. One is a principle; the other is an emotion. You act because of a scruple; you feel compunction.
The Tone and Register of the Word

Compunction is a formal word. You will see it more in serious writing — literature, journalism, formal speeches, essays — than in casual everyday conversation. Most people in everyday life would say "guilt," "remorse," or "feel bad" instead. But in formal or literary contexts, compunction is precise and carries a weight and gravity that simpler words sometimes lack.

• "He fired his loyal employees without compunction, thinking only of the numbers."
  • "She felt a sudden compunction after reading the letter she had written in anger."
  • "The surgeon described having no compunction about her decision — she knew she had made the right call."
  • "Even a small amount of compunction might have stopped him from going through with the deception."
  • "It was the quiet compunction that stayed with him for years, not the punishment."
Compunction = the moral guilt or unease of conscience you feel because of something wrong you did or are about to do — and when someone acts without compunction, they feel none of that guilt at all.
